system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2154-01-11 18:05:00 to 2154-01-14 13:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for bright red blood per rectum and new bruising, with a history of chronic myeloid leukemia, chronic graft-versus-host disease, and prior venous thromboembolism on Lovenox. Initial evaluation revealed anemia with a hemoglobin of 10.0 g/dL, which dropped to 26.8% hematocrit, prompting a transfusion of one unit of packed red blood cells with good response. The bleeding was attributed to Lovenox use, with hemorrhoids identified as the likely source during colonoscopy, along with a non-bleeding gastric ulcer and gastritis on EGD. Lovenox was held and later restarted at a reduced dose of 60 mg daily. Hyperglycemia was noted on admission with a glucose of 381 mg/dL and HbA1c of 8.5%, consistent with steroid-induced diabetes. She remained stable, with improvement in hemoglobin and glucose levels, and was discharged home in good condition with follow-up arranged.
problems: Chronic myeloid leukemia, without mention of having achieved remission
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Secondary diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, not stated as uncontrolled, or unspecified
Gastric ulcer, unspecified as acute or chronic, without mention of hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction
Adrenal cortical steroids causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ female with left flank pain.  Evaluation for renal
stones.

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to CT of the abdomen and pelvis from ___.

FINDINGS:  Two frontal images of the abdomen show no evidence of renal or
ureteral stones.  Surgical clips are noted in the right upper quadrant and
right lower quadrant.  There is more stool than expected in the ascending
colon, with no evidence of obstruction.  There is no pneumatosis or free gas. 
Degenerative changes of the lumbar spine are noted along with bony
demineralization.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of renal or ureteral stones.  Prominent stool in the
ascending colon.

HISTORY:  ___ female with a history of CML status post allogeneic
transplant with graft-versus-host disease and liver compromise, now with
failure to thrive and left flank pain.

STUDY:  CT of the torso with contrast; 100 cc of Omnipaque intravenous
contrast was administered without adverse reaction or complication.  Coronal
and sagittal reformatted images were also generated.

COMPARISON:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast from ___
and CTA of the chest from ___.

FINDINGS:

CHEST:  The visualized portion of the thyroid appears unremarkable.  There is
no axillary, hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy, although calcified lymph
nodes are present in the left hilar and low paraesophageal regions, compatible
with prior granulomatous disease.  The aorta is of normal caliber along its
course without evidence of dissection.  Incidental note is made of a common
origin of the brachiocephalic and left common carotid arteries, a normal
variant (2:14).  The pulmonary arterial trunk is of normal caliber with no
central filling defect.  Calcified atherosclerotic disease is present in the
coronary arteries.  There is no pleural or pericardial effusion.  The lungs
are clear of consolidation and a single calcified granuloma is present in the
right upper lobe measuring 4 mm in diameter (2:22).  

A new soft tissue nodule is present in the right breast measuring 17 x 15 mm;
and sits adjacent to a rounded 7 mm calcification (2:26).

ABDOMEN:  The liver shows no focal lesion or intrahepatic biliary dilatation. 
Clips within the gallbladder fossa are compatible with prior cholecystectomy. 
The spleen is normal in size.  An incidental note is made of a punctate
calcification within the posterior portion of the spleen, compatible with a
granuloma.  The pancreas shows no masses or peripancreatic collections and
mild-to-moderate fatty atrophy is present.  The adrenal glands are normal
appearing bilaterally.  The kidneys enhance with and excrete contrast
symmetrically without evidence of masses or obstruction.  The large and small
bowel show no evidence of obstruction or wall edema.  The aorta is of normal
caliber along its course.  The portal vein is patent.  No lymphadenopathy,
free air or free fluid is demonstrated.

PELVIS:  The bladder, uterus and rectum appear unremarkable.  Sigmoid
diverticulosis is present without evidence of diverticulitis.  A dropped clip
is present in the anterior pelvis, presumably from prior cholecystectomy
(2:105).  There is no free fluid or lymphadenopathy.

BONES:  There are no aggressive-appearing lytic or sclerotic lesions.  There
continues to be endplate sclerosis of the superior portion of L5 and to a
lesser degree the inferior portion of L4 with mild depression and irregularity
of the superior endplate of L5, similar to prior exam.  Old healing rib
fractures of the left lateral eighth, seventh, sixth and fifth ribs are
present (___).  Additionally, an old healing fracture of the posterior
right tenth rib is present (2:50).

IMPRESSION:

1.  No acute intrathoracic or intra-abdominal process.
2.  Subacute left rib fractures are likely the source of left sided pain.
3.  New right breast lesion for which mammographic evaluation is recommended.
4.  Sigmoid diverticulosis without diverticulitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having left flank pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been going on for about 15 days. It's sharp and constant, and it gets worse when I walk or take deep breaths.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Does the pain go anywhere else? Any burning with urination or blood in your urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it doesn’t radiate. And no, I haven’t noticed any issues with urination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned it feels similar to when you fell a while back. Is this the same area?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly the same spot on my left side. It went away before, but now it’s back and getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ll get some imaging done to check what’s going on. We’ll start with a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the scan show if it’s related to my bones or muscles?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it will help us see if there’s any fracture or other issue in the ribs or spine. Given your history, we want to be thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The initial images didn’t show kidney stones, which is good. But we need a more detailed scan with contrast to get a full picture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my other conditions? I’m on a lot of medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your meds, and the contrast should be safe. We’ll monitor you closely during the scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan with contrast is back. There’s no sign of an abdominal emergency, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan shows subacute fractures in your left ribs. These appear to be healing but still painful. That’s likely the source of your flank pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I did fall on that side a few weeks ago. But why is it flaring up now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes pain can return as you resume activity. The bones are healing, but they’re still sensitive to movement and pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, these don’t require surgery. We’ll manage the pain with medication and rest. We’ll also consult pain management for longer-term support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable. Anything else on the scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There is something we need to follow up on. A new soft tissue nodule was seen in your right breast, about 17 mm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A nodule? Is that cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t say for sure yet. It could be related to an old bruise you mentioned. But we recommend a mammogram to check it further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had some bruising there a while ago. Could that cause a nodule?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, trauma can sometimes cause benign changes. But we want to be safe and make sure it resolves. Your PCP will help coordinate the follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll make sure to follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed you’ve been having leg pain when walking. You mentioned it’s been going on for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it hurts when I walk, and it’s tender to touch. I thought it was just from the DVT I had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related to circulation. We recommend an ankle-brachial index test with exercise to check for peripheral vascular disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can do that after I’m discharged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s an outpatient test. We’ll send the order to your primary care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work is stable. Hemoglobin is improving, and liver enzymes are only slightly elevated, which we expect with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my prednisone? It was increased recently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping it at 40 mg for now due to your GVHD. But we’ll discuss tapering it with your specialist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve been worried about side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally valid. We’ll monitor your glucose and bone health closely, especially with your history of fractures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today. Pain is better controlled, and no new issues have come up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. What about the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with oxycodone for breakthrough pain and a new prescription for gabapentin, which helps with chronic nerve and bone pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reducing it to 30 mg daily. Please follow up with your oncologist to continue the taper safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the breast nodule?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please schedule a mammogram within the next month. Even if it’s from old bruising, we need to make sure it’s not persistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call my doctor right after I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re cleared to go home. Keep following up with your specialists, and call if the pain worsens or you have any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — should I avoid physical activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting or strenuous activity for a few weeks. Gentle walking is fine, but listen to your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep up with your follow-ups and take your meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll discharge your paperwork shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly with your prescriptions and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, thank you.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for left flank pain lasting 15 days, with a history of chronic myeloid leukemia, chronic graft-versus-host disease, and prior anticoagulant use. Imaging revealed subacute fractures in the left ribs, likely due to a previous fall, which explained the pain. A new soft tissue nodule in the right breast was incidentally found on CT and recommended for mammographic follow-up. The patient also reported bilateral leg pain with ambulation, suggestive of claudication, prompting a recommendation for outpatient ankle-brachial index testing. Pain was managed with oxycodone and gabapentin, and prednisone was tapered to 30 mg daily. The patient remained stable, with no acute abdominal process, and was discharged home with follow-up plans.
